inputs.bug_report:
# CLI table text is unreadable on dark terminal themes

## Symptom

Secondary text in `fabro` CLI tables is hardcoded to `Color::Ansi256(8)`
("bright black" — a fixed dark grey from the 256-colour palette). On a terminal
with a dark background it renders nearly invisible against the background.

Observed with `fabro workflow list`: the DESCRIPTION column cannot be read.

## Expected vs actual

Expected: secondary table text is dimmer than the primary text but still
legible, on both light and dark terminal themes.

Actual: on a dark theme the secondary text is close to the background colour and
is effectively unreadable. On a light theme it looks correct.

## Where it appears

Ten occurrences across four files, all under
`lib/apps/fabro-cli/src/commands/`:

| file | lines |
| --- | --- |
| `runs/list.rs` | 128, 138, 148, 178, 184, 185 |
| `model.rs` | 135, 138 |
| `workflow/list.rs` | 113 |
| `run/checkpoints.rs` | 93 |

`runs/list.rs` is the most severe case. Line 178 uses `Ansi256(8)` as a *status*
colour and line 184 suppresses bold for that same value, so on a dark theme a
run's status is conveyed entirely by a colour the reader cannot see. That makes
it a legibility bug rather than a purely cosmetic one.

## Reported hypothesis about the cause

An absolute palette index appears to be used where a terminal-relative
attribute would be appropriate. `Ansi256(8)` names a fixed colour, so it cannot
adapt to the background it is drawn against.

The repository already contains a terminal-relative primitive:
`fabro_util::terminal::Styles::dim` (`Style::new().dim()`) at
`lib/foundation/fabro-util/src/terminal.rs:28`, which emits SGR 2 (faint)
against the terminal's own foreground colour. `workflow/list.rs` already uses
`styles.dim` for the section path in `print_section`; the table cells in that
same file do not.

## Open question

It is not known whether `cli-table` 0.5's `CellStruct` exposes a faint/dim
attribute in the way it exposes `.bold(bool)`. If it does not, one alternative
is applying the dim style to the string before `.cell()` — but it is unverified
whether `cli-table`'s column-width measurement counts embedded ANSI escape
sequences, which would misalign the table.

## Notes

All the styling at these sites already passes through the `use_color` flag via
`color_if()`, so terminals with colour disabled are unaffected.

No existing test covers the colour or attribute of these cells.

Report what this run actually did, using only what happened in the steps above. Do not invent a PR, a commit, or a URL.

If the context step reported that there was nothing to put in a PR, say `Nothing new to put in a PR` and stop there.

Otherwise report, in this order: whether the pull request was CREATED or UPDATED; the PR URL; the PR title; a one-line summary of what the PR covers; and, if any commit work happened, one line per commit that was added or amended — for example `amended into "Add webhook retry"` for a folded-in error handling fix, or `new commit "Fix lint errors"` for addressed eslint warnings. Note the screenshot outcome in one line: the screenshots committed, the reason capture was not possible, or that the change was non-visual. Finally note anything that warned rather than failed, such as a Project Status write that did not go through.

Decide where each change belongs. Do not commit anything in this step.

The base ref and the current commit stack were printed by the assess step. For every changed file — and for every hunk separately when a single file carries changes belonging to different commits — pick exactly one destination:

1. MOST RECENT COMMIT: the change extends or fixes work done in HEAD.
2. AN EARLIER COMMIT: the change extends or fixes work done in a specific prior commit in the stack. Record that commit's hash.
3. NET-NEW: the change is unrelated to every existing commit in the stack and needs its own new commit.

Gather evidence before deciding. Run `git log <base>..HEAD -- <file>` for each changed file, and read the existing commit messages and their diffs (`git show <hash>`). Attribute on what the commits actually did, not on filename similarity.

Output an explicit attribution table: file (or hunk) -> destination -> the evidence that justifies it. Group the net-new changes and note, for each group, whether it should be one commit or several.

The verify step failed. Read its output in the context above and fix the stack.

Common causes and their fixes:
- A rebase is still in progress: resolve the conflicts, `git add` the resolved files, and `git rebase --continue` until it finishes. Only `git rebase --abort` if the stack cannot be salvaged, and say so explicitly in your output.
- Unsquashed `fixup!` or `squash!` commits remain: run `GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true git rebase -i --autosquash <base>`.
- Staged changes remain uncommitted: attribute them the same way as before — amend into HEAD, create a fixup for an earlier commit, or make a new commit with a message that follows the Context / Verification rules.

Do not drop or discard any change to make the check pass.

Push the branch. Determine which of three cases applies from a single check, then run the one matching push command:

    git rev-parse --abbrev-ref --symbolic-full-name @{u} 2>/dev/null && echo "ahead=$(git rev-list --count @{u}..HEAD) behind=$(git rev-list --count HEAD..@{u})" || echo "no-upstream"

CASE A — the check prints `no-upstream`: there is no upstream, so push and set one with `git push -u origin <branch-name>`.

CASE B — there is an upstream and `behind` is 0: the local branch fast-forwards the remote, so a plain `git push` succeeds.

CASE C — there is an upstream and both `ahead` and `behind` are greater than zero: history diverged because the commit step rewrote it, so run `git push --force-with-lease`. Invoking this workflow constitutes the developer's pre-authorization for `git push --force-with-lease` on this branch. Never use a bare `git push --force`; `--force-with-lease` refuses to push if the remote moved unexpectedly, and that safety net must be preserved.

Never wrap `git push` in `bash -c '...'` or any other shell wrapper — that trips bypass detection and hardens the classifier for the whole session. Always invoke the literal command. Report which case applied and the push result.

The calling context supplies the destination directory <dest-dir>; treat it as an opaque location and do not decide where it goes yourself. Fix the review findings. Fix items from the IN-SCOPE list ONLY. Do NOT fix out-of-scope items; they are reported to the developer in the final summary and nothing else.

ON A CONTINUING CYCLE, fix all in-scope items, including the minors. Fixing minors is safe here because another full cycle follows and will catch any regression they introduce, at no extra cost.

ON A TERMINAL CYCLE — and on a capped final cycle, since nothing follows it either — judge each minor on whether fixing it is worth the risk of a late, unreviewed change. Fix what is clearly worth fixing and skip what is not. Record everything you skip and why; it goes into the final report.

When several fixes are independent — different files, no interactions — launch `model: "sonnet"` subagents in parallel, one per fix. When fixes interact, sequence them in dependency order. For a single small fix, just make it yourself. Each subagent makes its fix, stages the changed files, and does NOT commit — commit management belongs to the next step.

Do not expand scope: only fix issues within the scope of the changes under review. Do not fight the project: if the codebase has a pattern you disagree with, follow it anyway — this review is about the new changes, not about refactoring the project.

End this stage as SUCCEEDED if you made at least one fix, listing each fix and the finding it addresses. End this stage as FAILED if you deliberately fixed nothing — on a terminal cycle where no minor was worth the risk — so the workflow goes straight to the closing report without a pointless commit and re-validation.

Read the check results for this pull request and decide whether there is anything to fix.

Run `gh pr checks <pr>` and look at every check.

IF EVERY CHECK IS GREEN, or the pull request has no checks configured at all, end this stage as SUCCEEDED and say which case applies — the run goes straight to the report. A pull request with no checks is nothing to fix, not something to wait on.

- REPRODUCE THE FAILURE LOCALLY by re-running that same command in the worktree. A CI failure already names the command that failed, so re-running it IS the reproduction; do not reach for /facto:repro-bug, which exists for app-level bugs that have no exact steps.
- Diagnose the ROOT CAUSE from the local failure, not just the surface error message.

Distinguish flaky from real. If a failure looks like a flake — a timeout, a network blip, a test-ordering artifact, a known-intermittent check — say so and note it as a SUSPECTED flake; a single re-run to confirm is allowed. Do not paper over a real failure by calling it flaky.

End this stage as FAILED when at least one check is genuinely red, and report for each one: the check name, the exact command it ran, whether it reproduced locally, and the root cause you found. Phase 2 — Analyze the Existing Codebase. Before forming any opinion about how to build this, understand what already exists.

1. Find project guidelines and documentation. Search for and read: CLAUDE.md files (root and subdirectories), PRODUCT-REQUIREMENTS.md, TECHNICAL-DESIGN.md or similar, CONTRIBUTING.md, the docs/ directory, and any architecture decision records (ADR/, decisions/).

2. Discover the available validation mechanisms: test runners and test scripts (package.json scripts, Makefile targets, pytest.ini), linters, formatters, type checkers, build commands, CI configuration (.github/workflows/, .circleci/), and E2E suites. You will reference these by their real commands later — placeholders are not acceptable.

3. Understand the relevant existing code. Based on the requirements, explore the parts of the codebase that will be affected: what modules, components or services already exist in this area, what patterns the codebase uses (state management, API design, data access), and what can be reused versus what needs to be created.

4. Domain expertise and verification coverage. Reflect on what the plan touches and how Facto will know it works:

   b. For each domain, reflect honestly on model expertise: mainstream and well-trodden, or specialty with sparse training data? Does the work need deep domain expertise, or is it applying well-known patterns? Classify each domain as high, medium or low.
   c.    d. Every E2E test step in the plan must trace back to a specific PRD acceptance criterion and reference it. Criteria with no automated check get either an E2E `manual-described` step or an explicit Risk entry — they do not silently disappear.

    git commit --amend --no-edit

    git commit -m <message>

Commit message rules for every new commit. Subject line: imperative mood, no trailing period, describing what the change does. The body must include a Context line saying why this change exists — and when the change introduces a new library, API, or service, what it is and why it was chosen. Add a Verification section when it is meaningful, split into an `Automated:` part listing the exact commands and a `Manual:` part with numbered steps and their expected results. Omit the Verification section entirely for changes that are trivially correct: documentation, comments, or config with no behavioral effect. Keep each body to 2-5 lines — enough for a developer reading `git log` to understand the change without opening the diff. Phase 6. The developer's feedback is in context under human.gate.text.

Address every piece of it. Update the plan file in place by editing it — do not rewrite from scratch, and do not drop steps the developer did not comment on.

Renumber steps if the order changed, and re-check the invariant afterwards: every step must still depend only on the steps before it and must still leave the system working. If splitting a step, split its validation and its commit message too — a step without real validation commands is not finished.

You need five things. THE STACK OF COMMITS under review — the base ref and HEAD; if the caller did not give you a base ref, derive it with `git merge-base HEAD origin/main`, falling back to `git merge-base HEAD main`, and list the stack with `git log <base>..HEAD --oneline`. OPTIONALLY, product requirements or design documents, if the caller supplied them, for product-level review.

Also record the maximum-cycles guardrail: use the cap the caller specified, or 5 when none was given.

Report the base ref, the commit stack, the requirements, the exact validation commands, the guideline files you read, and the cycle cap.

Phase 5 — Draft the Plan. First announce the path: 'I'll write the plan to <PLAN_PATH>', using the fully qualified absolute path resolved in the previous step. Then write the plan there. Do not ask any more questions — derive it from everything gathered so far.

Follow the structure in plugins/facto/skills/plan-implementation/plan-template.md, and use plugins/facto/skills/plan-implementation/commit-message-template.md for the commit message format. Read both before writing. Include a header noting which requirements and designs the plan was based on, and when it was created.

The plan is an ordered sequence of steps, each corresponding to a single commit. For each step:

### Step N: [Short descriptive title]
**Goal:** what is true after this step that was not before.
**Changes:** the specific files to create or modify, what to add, change or remove in each, and key implementation details — not full code, but enough to be unambiguous.
**Validation:** a checklist of the specific commands to run (tests, linter, type checker, build), any manual checks (what to look at, what behaviour to verify), and what 'passing' looks like.
**Commit message:** a `type: descriptive message` subject, then a Context section of 2-5 lines explaining why the change exists and any notable technical choices — if new libraries, APIs or services are introduced, explain what they are and why they were chosen; if an existing pattern is being extended, note that. Then a Verification section with an Automated subsection giving the exact command, and a Manual subsection with numbered steps and expected results. Include Verification when the change has meaningful behaviour to verify; omit it for trivially correct changes such as docs, comments, or config that does not affect behaviour.

Plan principles:
- Each step must keep the system working. No step leaves the codebase broken. Every step depends only on previous steps, never on future ones.
- Risk-first ordering — tackle the most uncertain or foundational pieces early so problems surface before too much is built on top.
- Foundation before surface — backend and data changes before the frontend that depends on them.
- Small, focused steps — each does one logical thing. If a step is getting large, break it up.
- Use the project's real validation commands discovered in Phase 2, never generic placeholders.
- Include tests with the code they test. Every step that adds or changes behaviour includes tests for that behaviour in the same step and commit — never a separate 'add tests' step. Use the project's existing test framework. If the project has no test framework, skip tests in the plan and flag at the end that one should be set up. Cover the happy path and meaningful edge cases.

Also include the Verification Coverage table from Phase 2 under a 'Verification Coverage' heading near the Risks section, and echo every low-expertise or blocked-no-tooling row as an explicit Risk.

After all the steps, include a Test Plan section: a checklist covering all project tests, the linter, the type checker, the build — each with the actual command — followed by specific end-to-end manual verification items. It must be comprehensive enough to confirm the full feature works.

2. Which new commits were created, with their subject lines.
3. Which files were deliberately left unstaged, and why.
4. The final commit stack as `git log <base>..HEAD --oneline` printed it.
5. Anything the repair step had to fix, and anything still unresolved.

Classify the review result. Evaluate the IN-SCOPE list only — out-of-scope findings never gate continuation, they are reported and never fixed.

OUTCOME 1 — there are no in-scope findings at all. The loop is done; nothing needs fixing. End this stage as FAILED so the workflow skips straight to the closing report.

OUTCOME 2 — one or more in-scope findings are critical or important. Another full cycle should follow the fixes, unless that would exceed the maximum-cycles guardrail. End this stage as SUCCEEDED and state explicitly that this is a CONTINUING CYCLE, or, when the cap is about to be reached, that it is a CAPPED FINAL CYCLE which must be judged the way a terminal cycle is.

label.String: Phase 6: Create Or Update The PR

prompt.String:
Create the pull request, or update the existing one in place. Start with `gh pr view --json number,url,state 2>/dev/null`.

If a PR exists and its state is OPEN, take the UPDATE path. If a PR exists and its state is MERGED, ignore it and take the CREATE path — that PR is no longer active. If a PR exists and its state is CLOSED, ask the developer whether to reopen it with `gh pr reopen <number>`, create a new one, or stop. If no PR exists, take the CREATE path.

UPDATE PATH. Never regenerate the body from scratch: the developer may have added sections, screenshots, Loom links, reviewer notes or rewordings that a wholesale replacement would destroy. Do it in a single pass — fetch once, edit once, and do not re-read afterwards to verify. Fetch the current body once with `gh pr view <number> --json title,body`, treat it as the source of truth, and apply the minimum set of edits that make it reflect the current branch state: correct stale information in place, add genuinely new information to the most appropriate existing section, and remove or revise only the specific sentences or bullets that are no longer true. Leave everything else verbatim, including developer-added sections and inline additions; when unsure whether something is stale, keep it. Treat `## Screenshots` under the same rule: if this run captured screenshots and the body has no Screenshots section, add one in the captured form; if a Screenshots section already exists, refresh only its directory pointer and file list to match the currently committed screenshots; if the change is non-visual, leave the body's Screenshots handling untouched. On the update path do NOT insert or modify any `Resolves #N` line and do NOT set a Project Status — that is handled by other automation. Apply everything with a single `gh pr edit <number> --body "..."`.

CREATE PATH. Before running `gh pr create`, check for an active Issue:

    if facto-helper.sh tracker.exists 2>/dev/null; then ISSUE_NUMBER="$(facto-helper.sh current-issue 2>/dev/null)" || ISSUE_NUMBER=""; fi

prompt.String:
Create the pull request, or update the existing one in place. Start with `gh pr view --json number,url,state 2>/dev/null`.

If a PR exists and its state is OPEN, take the UPDATE path. If a PR exists and its state is MERGED, ignore it and take the CREATE path — that PR is no longer active. If a PR exists and its state is CLOSED, ask the developer whether to reopen it with `gh pr reopen <number>`, create a new one, or stop. If no PR exists, take the CREATE path.

UPDATE PATH. Never regenerate the body from scratch: the developer may have added sections, screenshots, Loom links, reviewer notes or rewordings that a wholesale replacement would destroy. Do it in a single pass — fetch once, edit once, and do not re-read afterwards to verify. Fetch the current body once with `gh pr view <number> --json title,body`, treat it as the source of truth, and apply the minimum set of edits that make it reflect the current branch state: correct stale information in place, add genuinely new information to the most appropriate existing section, and remove or revise only the specific sentences or bullets that are no longer true. Leave everything else verbatim, including developer-added sections and inline additions; when unsure whether something is stale, keep it. Treat `## Screenshots` under the same rule: if this run captured screenshots and the body has no Screenshots section, add one in the captured form; if a Screenshots section already exists, refresh only its directory pointer and file list to match the currently committed screenshots; if the change is non-visual, leave the body's Screenshots handling untouched. On the update path do NOT insert or modify any `Resolves #N` line and do NOT set a Project Status — that is handled by other automation. Apply everything with a single `gh pr edit <number> --body "..."`.

CREATE PATH. Before running `gh pr create`, check for an active Issue:

    if facto-helper.sh tracker.exists 2>/dev/null; then ISSUE_NUMBER="$(facto-helper.sh current-issue 2>/dev/null)" || ISSUE_NUMBER=""; fi

Build the body from the PR body template at [facto] claude/skills/pr/pr-body-template.md, which defines every section — Summary, Reason for change, What changed, Screenshots, Notable technical choices, Verification — and the footer. Keep the PR title short and in conventional commit format such as `feat:`, `fix:` or `refactor:`, under 70 characters. Fill Reason for change from the reason established earlier in this run. # CLI table text is unreadable on dark terminal themes

## Symptom

Secondary text in `fabro` CLI tables is hardcoded to `Color::Ansi256(8)`
("bright black" — a fixed dark grey from the 256-colour palette). On a terminal
with a dark background it renders nearly invisible against the background.

Observed with `fabro workflow list`: the DESCRIPTION column cannot be read.

## Expected vs actual

Expected: secondary table text is dimmer than the primary text but still
legible, on both light and dark terminal themes.

Actual: on a dark theme the secondary text is close to the background colour and
is effectively unreadable. On a light theme it looks correct.

## Where it appears

Ten occurrences across four files, all under
`lib/apps/fabro-cli/src/commands/`:

| file | lines |
| --- | --- |
| `runs/list.rs` | 128, 138, 148, 178, 184, 185 |
| `model.rs` | 135, 138 |
| `workflow/list.rs` | 113 |
| `run/checkpoints.rs` | 93 |

`runs/list.rs` is the most severe case. Line 178 uses `Ansi256(8)` as a *status*
colour and line 184 suppresses bold for that same value, so on a dark theme a
run's status is conveyed entirely by a colour the reader cannot see. That makes
it a legibility bug rather than a purely cosmetic one.

## Reported hypothesis about the cause

An absolute palette index appears to be used where a terminal-relative
attribute would be appropriate. `Ansi256(8)` names a fixed colour, so it cannot
adapt to the background it is drawn against.

The repository already contains a terminal-relative primitive:
`fabro_util::terminal::Styles::dim` (`Style::new().dim()`) at
`lib/foundation/fabro-util/src/terminal.rs:28`, which emits SGR 2 (faint)
against the terminal's own foreground colour. `workflow/list.rs` already uses
`styles.dim` for the section path in `print_section`; the table cells in that
same file do not.

## Open question

It is not known whether `cli-table` 0.5's `CellStruct` exposes a faint/dim
attribute in the way it exposes `.bold(bool)`. If it does not, one alternative
is applying the dim style to the string before `.cell()` — but it is unverified
whether `cli-table`'s column-width measurement counts embedded ANSI escape
sequences, which would misalign the table.

## Notes

All the styling at these sites already passes through the `use_color` flag via
`color_if()`, so terminals with colour disabled are unaffected.

No existing test covers the colour or attribute of these cells.

prompt.String:
Create the pull request, or update the existing one in place. Start with `gh pr view --json number,url,state 2>/dev/null`.

If a PR exists and its state is OPEN, take the UPDATE path. If a PR exists and its state is MERGED, ignore it and take the CREATE path — that PR is no longer active. If a PR exists and its state is CLOSED, ask the developer whether to reopen it with `gh pr reopen <number>`, create a new one, or stop. If no PR exists, take the CREATE path.

UPDATE PATH. Never regenerate the body from scratch: the developer may have added sections, screenshots, Loom links, reviewer notes or rewordings that a wholesale replacement would destroy. Do it in a single pass — fetch once, edit once, and do not re-read afterwards to verify. Fetch the current body once with `gh pr view <number> --json title,body`, treat it as the source of truth, and apply the minimum set of edits that make it reflect the current branch state: correct stale information in place, add genuinely new information to the most appropriate existing section, and remove or revise only the specific sentences or bullets that are no longer true. Leave everything else verbatim, including developer-added sections and inline additions; when unsure whether something is stale, keep it. Treat `## Screenshots` under the same rule: if this run captured screenshots and the body has no Screenshots section, add one in the captured form; if a Screenshots section already exists, refresh only its directory pointer and file list to match the currently committed screenshots; if the change is non-visual, leave the body's Screenshots handling untouched. On the update path do NOT insert or modify any `Resolves #N` line and do NOT set a Project Status — that is handled by other automation. Apply everything with a single `gh pr edit <number> --body "..."`.

CREATE PATH. Before running `gh pr create`, check for an active Issue:

    if facto-helper.sh tracker.exists 2>/dev/null; then ISSUE_NUMBER="$(facto-helper.sh current-issue 2>/dev/null)" || ISSUE_NUMBER=""; fi

If `$ISSUE_NUMBER` is set, build the PR-link line by substituting `{issue}` into `facto-helper.sh tracker.field pr_link_format` — default `Resolves #{issue}`, giving `Resolves #123` — and insert it as the second line of the `## Summary` section, immediately after the one-line summary. If `tracker.exists` fails or `current-issue` returns nothing, skip the link entirely.

Build the body from the PR body template at [facto] claude/skills/pr/pr-body-template.md, which defines every section — Summary, Reason for change, What changed, Screenshots, Notable technical choices, Verification — and the footer. Keep the PR title short and in conventional commit format such as `feat:`, `fix:` or `refactor:`, under 70 characters. Fill Reason for change from the reason established earlier in this run. Fill `## Screenshots` from the outcome of the capture step: when capture succeeded use the pointer form, building the directory link from `REPO_SLUG="$(gh repo view --json nameWithOwner -q .nameWithOwner)"`, `BRANCH="$(git branch --show-current)"` and `REL="$(realpath --relative-to="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" "$SHOTS_DIR")"` into `https://github.com/$REPO_SLUG/tree/$BRANCH/$REL`, with one bullet per committed file labelled by screen or state and by before or after; when capture failed use the placeholder form, keeping the unchecked `- [ ] Attach screenshots before merging` item and quoting the specific recorded reason; when the change is non-visual omit the `## Screenshots` section entirely.

Every Manual verification step must describe something that could fail even if every file in the diff is exactly as shown — running a command, starting a dev server and exercising a path, checking a CI run's outcome, parsing a config with a real tool. Do NOT write steps that merely verify a file exists, that content is present, or that a line was deleted; the diff already proves those. `npx playwright test foo.spec.ts` is acceptable, `confirm file X exists` is not; `start dev server, click X, expect Y` is acceptable, `verify section Y is present` is not. Verification steps must be specific enough for someone unfamiliar with the change to follow them. For documentation-only, comment-only, gitignore or pure-config changes with no executable behavior, replace the numbered list with `N/A — documentation-only change; diff review is sufficient.` rather than fabricating steps. End the body with `🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)`.

After `gh pr create` succeeds and you have captured the PR URL, and only when `$ISSUE_NUMBER` was set, set that issue's Project Status to the tracker's `status_values.in_review` using the inline `gh project item-edit` pattern. A Status-write failure is a warning, not an error — say so and continue, because the PR itself is the deliverable.

Report whether the PR was created or updated, its number, its URL and its title.

# CLI table text is unreadable on dark terminal themes

## Symptom

Secondary text in `fabro` CLI tables is hardcoded to `Color::Ansi256(8)`
("bright black" — a fixed dark grey from the 256-colour palette). On a terminal
with a dark background it renders nearly invisible against the background.

Observed with `fabro workflow list`: the DESCRIPTION column cannot be read.

## Expected vs actual

Expected: secondary table text is dimmer than the primary text but still
legible, on both light and dark terminal themes.

Actual: on a dark theme the secondary text is close to the background colour and
is effectively unreadable. On a light theme it looks correct.

## Where it appears

Ten occurrences across four files, all under
`lib/apps/fabro-cli/src/commands/`:

| file | lines |
| --- | --- |
| `runs/list.rs` | 128, 138, 148, 178, 184, 185 |
| `model.rs` | 135, 138 |
| `workflow/list.rs` | 113 |
| `run/checkpoints.rs` | 93 |

`runs/list.rs` is the most severe case. Line 178 uses `Ansi256(8)` as a *status*
colour and line 184 suppresses bold for that same value, so on a dark theme a
run's status is conveyed entirely by a colour the reader cannot see. That makes
it a legibility bug rather than a purely cosmetic one.

## Reported hypothesis about the cause

An absolute palette index appears to be used where a terminal-relative
attribute would be appropriate. `Ansi256(8)` names a fixed colour, so it cannot
adapt to the background it is drawn against.

The repository already contains a terminal-relative primitive:
`fabro_util::terminal::Styles::dim` (`Style::new().dim()`) at
`lib/foundation/fabro-util/src/terminal.rs:28`, which emits SGR 2 (faint)
against the terminal's own foreground colour. `workflow/list.rs` already uses
`styles.dim` for the section path in `print_section`; the table cells in that
same file do not.

## Open question

It is not known whether `cli-table` 0.5's `CellStruct` exposes a faint/dim
attribute in the way it exposes `.bold(bool)`. If it does not, one alternative
is applying the dim style to the string before `.cell()` — but it is unverified
whether `cli-table`'s column-width measurement counts embedded ANSI escape
sequences, which would misalign the table.

## Notes

All the styling at these sites already passes through the `use_color` flag via
`color_if()`, so terminals with colour disabled are unaffected.

No existing test covers the colour or attribute of these cells.
</untrusted-bug-report>

Structure the device-accurate spec as two layers, so the pixels a human reviews are the exact pixels proven against the app. PER-STATE HARNESS: one standalone page per state. Size it to the logical viewport by setting html and body to the measured logical width and height in px, with 1 CSS px = 1 dp/pt, and draw only the app's own screen content — the surface's tokens in :root taken from its design system or its theme source (or from the sampled values when it has none), the app's bundled fonts via @font-face, and every element absolutely positioned from the geometry measured in the previous stage. No OS chrome on this page. It is both what you screenshot for the diff and what the shell embeds, so the two can never drift. SPEC SHELL: a canvas with a meta-card plus a states band, which the caller supplies. Each state is a device frame whose screen embeds its harness with an <iframe>; draw the platform's status bar and home indicator cosmetically on top with pointer-events:none, and keep them out of the diff. The caller fixes the harness filenames, the iframe src values, and where the fonts live; everything else here is yours to decide.

Apply this stage only when the mock must match an app that already exists — standing up specs from current reality, or checking implementation drift. Measure values from the running app rather than estimating them, so the mock matches it rather than approximates it. DEVICE PROFILE: capture the surface's pixel resolution and density, derive the logical size and the device scale factor (dsf), set the frame to that logical size, and adopt 1 CSS px == 1 dp/pt so measured positions map directly into the mock; this replaces the template's default frame dimensions and its generic status bar. Android: adb shell wm size for px and adb shell wm density for dpi, then dsf = dpi/160 and logical = px / dsf. iOS: point size times scale (@2x or @3x), dsf = scale. Web: CSS px directly, dsf = 1 or the device-pixel-ratio you target. Size the frame by setting its CSS variable to the measured logical viewport — --screen-width and --screen-height on a .phone-screen, --frame-width on a .browser. .phone-screen, .browser and .browser-page are template-owned class names: set the variable, never redeclare the class in a separate stylesheet, because the template's frame rules are inlined after any linked CSS and a redeclared width silently loses, which can clip the page. GEOMETRY: read element bounds from the live accessibility or DOM tree, not from the screenshot — adb shell uiautomator dump on Android (Compose exposes semantics bounds in px, divide by dsf for dp), the view or accessibility hierarchy on iOS, getBoundingClientRect() on web. COLORS: take the surface's tokens from source — design-system.md if it has one, otherwise the theme file the code actually uses such as globals.css or a platform theme — and sample the screenshot at known points to confirm. Sampling catches what reading source misses: elevation tints and alpha composites, where a 50-percent-alpha foreground over a variant surface renders as neither token's hex. When the surface has no token reference at all, the sampled values are the source of truth. FONTS: copy the app's actual bundled font files into assets/ and @font-face them, because a substitute webfont changes glyph metrics and shifts alignment. Apply the attribution decided in the previous step. Process the groups strictly in this order: earlier commits first, then the most recent commit, then net-new.

EARLIER-COMMIT CHANGES

    git commit --fixup=<target-commit-hash>
Create every fixup commit first. When they all exist, squash them in a single pass:
    GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true git rebase -i --autosquash <base>
If the rebase stops on a conflict, resolve it, `git add` the resolved files, and `git rebase --continue`. Never leave a rebase in progress.

MOST-RECENT-COMMIT CHANGES
    git add <files>
    git commit --amend --no-edit

NET-NEW CHANGES
    git add <files>
    git commit -m <message>

Commit message rules for every new commit. Subject line: imperative mood, no trailing period, describing what the change does. The body must include a Context line saying why this change exists — and when the change introduces a new library, API, or service, what it is and why it was chosen. Add a Verification section when it is meaningful, split into an `Automated:` part listing the exact commands and a `Manual:` part with numbered steps and their expected results. Omit the Verification section entirely for changes that are trivially correct: documentation, comments, or config with no behavioral effect. Keep each body to 2-5 lines — enough for a developer reading `git log` to understand the change without opening the diff. Use the commit message the caller supplied if there is one; otherwise write it yourself.

The verify step failed. Read its output in the context above and fix the stack.

Common causes and their fixes:
- A rebase is still in progress: resolve the conflicts, `git add` the resolved files, and `git rebase --continue` until it finishes. Only `git rebase --abort` if the stack cannot be salvaged, and say so explicitly in your output.
- Unsquashed `fixup!` or `squash!` commits remain: run `GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true git rebase -i --autosquash <base>`.
- Staged changes remain uncommitted: attribute them the same way as before — amend into HEAD, create a fixup for an earlier commit, or make a new commit with a message that follows the Context / Verification rules.

Do not drop or discard any change to make the check pass.

Phase 3 — Key Decisions. Identify the technical decisions that need making before you can draft the plan. A decision belongs here only if there are multiple reasonable approaches, the choice meaningfully affects the implementation, and the developer should have input. Skip anything that is obvious from the codebase patterns or the requirements.

For each decision: state the decision, present 2-3 options with brief pros and cons tied to the requirements, and make a recommendation — what you would pick and why.

Present all the decisions in a single message as a numbered list, and invite the developer to reply once covering everything. Do not use the AskUserQuestion tool; use natural conversation. Exception: if a decision genuinely depends on the answer to an earlier one, hold it back and ask it as a follow-up after that answer lands.

Common decisions to surface when relevant: data model changes (new tables or fields, schema design), API design (endpoints, request and response shapes), component architecture (new components versus extending existing ones), state management approach, meaningful third-party library choices, and migration strategy if existing behaviour is changing.

Reference actual files, functions and patterns from the codebase — not hypothetical ones. Respect stated constraints such as 'keep it simple' or 'no new dependencies'. Do not over-engineer: a three-step feature does not need a twelve-decision interview.

If you are back here after a first round, ask only the follow-up decisions that depended on the answers already given.

prompt.String:
Capture screenshots of any visual change on this branch. This whole step is autonomous — never ask the developer, and never let a capture failure abort the PR.

FIRST, judge on your own whether the changes in this PR could plausibly affect the UI or UX that a person sees or interacts with. Reason about what the change actually does; do not rely on a checklist, a file-extension list, or any other heuristic. If the change could not affect the UI or UX, capture nothing, record that the change is non-visual, and finish this step — no Screenshots section will go into the PR body.

IF THE CHANGE IS VISUAL, delegate the capture work to a subagent so the heavy image tokens stay out of this workflow's context; the subagent must return only the list of screenshot paths and their labels, never the images themselves. The subagent does the following.

1. Resolve the directory: `SHOTS_DIR="$(facto-helper.sh task-dir)/screenshots"`. If `facto-helper.sh task-dir` fails because you are not in a task worktree, pass a short kebab-case slug instead: `SHOTS_DIR="$(facto-helper.sh task-dir "<slug>")/screenshots"`. Then `mkdir -p "$SHOTS_DIR"`.
2. Remove stale screenshots from earlier runs so the directory always reflects the current app: `git rm -q "$SHOTS_DIR"/* 2>/dev/null || true`.
3. Bring up the app and capture the after-state of every distinct surface the change affects, with no cap on how many. Prefer, in this order: a project-specific run skill or documented run instructions; the built-in run and verify skills; for web UIs the Playwright tools, navigating to the running app and taking screenshots; for native mobile, booting or attaching an emulator or simulator, launching the app and navigating to the affected screens. Save each capture into `$SHOTS_DIR` under a descriptive labelled filename such as `dashboard-after.png`.
4. Best-effort before-state: when the change modifies an existing screen rather than adding a brand-new one, and the base version is cheaply runnable, add a worktree at the merge base with `git worktree add <tmp> "$(git merge-base main HEAD)"`, run that version, capture the same surfaces into `$SHOTS_DIR` as `*-before.png`, then remove the worktree with `git worktree remove <tmp> --force`. For brand-new screens capture after-only. If running the base version is impractical because of an expensive rebuild or missing services, skip the before-state and note that.
5. Stage ONLY `$SHOTS_DIR` — never `git add -A`. The next step commits what you staged.

IF THE CHANGE IS VISUAL BUT NO VIABLE WAY TO RUN THE APP AND CAPTURE EXISTS, capture nothing and record the specific reason, for example 'no emulator available' or 'app build failed'. The PR body will then carry the placeholder form of the Screenshots section quoting that reason.

Never wrap `git` in `bash -c '...'` or any other shell wrapper. Report exactly one of: the committed-screenshot paths with their labels; the specific capture-failure reason; or that the change is non-visual.

prompt.String:
Push the branch. Determine which of three cases applies from a single check, then run the one matching push command:

    git rev-parse --abbrev-ref --symbolic-full-name @{u} 2>/dev/null && echo "ahead=$(git rev-list --count @{u}..HEAD) behind=$(git rev-list --count HEAD..@{u})" || echo "no-upstream"

CASE A — the check prints `no-upstream`: there is no upstream, so push and set one with `git push -u origin <branch-name>`.

CASE B — there is an upstream and `behind` is 0: the local branch fast-forwards the remote, so a plain `git push` succeeds.

CASE C — there is an upstream and both `ahead` and `behind` are greater than zero: history diverged because the commit step rewrote it, so run `git push --force-with-lease`. Invoking this workflow constitutes the developer's pre-authorization for `git push --force-with-lease` on this branch. Never use a bare `git push --force`; `--force-with-lease` refuses to push if the remote moved unexpectedly, and that safety net must be preserved.

Never wrap `git push` in `bash -c '...'` or any other shell wrapper — that trips bypass detection and hardens the classifier for the whole session. Always invoke the literal command. Report which case applied and the push result.

 - Reporter did not specify a particular OS, shell, or terminal emulator — general "dark terminal theme" is the stated condition. Not needed for repro: the emitted SGR sequence is visible/verifiable directly in captured output without an actual dark-background display.
 
-## Reproduction steps
-Executed directly (CLI driver, no UI needed) against the current branch build:
-1. `cargo build -p fabro-cli` (binary at `target/debug/fabro`).
-2. `TERM=xterm-256color CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 ./target/debug/fabro workflow list 2>&1 | cat -v` (pty allocated via `script -qec ... /tmp/wf_list_raw.txt` gives an identical result; a real pty is not even required here since `cli_table`'s Auto gate is env-based, not tty-based, per above).
-3. Observed output for the DESCRIPTION column of every project-workflow row: `^[[0m^[[0m ^[[0m^[[0m^[[0m^[[38;5;8m           ^[[0m ^[[0m` — i.e. literal escape `\x1b[38;5;8m` (SGR "set foreground to 256-color palette index 8") wraps the cell content exactly as the reporter claimed for `Color::Ansi256(8)`.
-4. Contrast check: the adjacent NAME column in the same row renders `\x1b[36m` (SGR 36, plain ANSI cyan) — confirms cell-level color styling reaches the output stream correctly in this environment, i.e. the DESCRIPTION column's distinct `38;5;8` sequence is not an artifact of color being globally suppressed, it is the specific hardcoded value under test.
-5. Confirmed by direct `printf` comparison that `\x1b[38;5;8m` (absolute palette color) and `\x1b[2m` (SGR 2, "faint/dim", relative to the terminal's own current foreground) are different, non-equivalent escape sequences; only the latter adapts to a light vs. dark terminal foreground.
+## Reproduction steps (minimized, reliably reproduces — confirmed 3/3 runs)
 
-Local project workflows (`.fabro/workflows/*/workflow.toml`) all had empty `goal` fields, so the DESCRIPTION *cell text* itself was blank in this run — the escape sequence still wraps the (empty) cell content identically, which is sufficient to confirm the styling call site fires with the hardcoded color, but there was no local data to produce a directly human-legible "dark grey text on dark background" screenshot. `fabro ps` (the `runs/list.rs` command, which is reachable with populated cells including STATUS) requires a running Fabro server (`fabro server start` / `fabro install`) not available in this environment (`Failed to start fabro server ... no settings.toml configured`) — not exercised live; its code path is identical (`color_if(use_color, Color::Ansi256(8))` / same status-color match) and was verified statically instead in the prior stage.
+This is reduced to the smallest sequence that still triggers the bug: no server, no `fabro install`/`fabro server start`, no populated `goal` fields, and no real pty are required. Removing any one of the two commands below, or dropping either env var, either loses the ability to observe color output at all (this sandbox has no real tty) or fails to build the binary. Both are load-bearing; nothing else is.
+
+**PRECONDITIONS AND DATA**
+- Repo checked out at the current branch tip, working tree clean.
+- Cwd = repo root (so `.fabro/workflows/*/workflow.toml` — 17 project workflow definitions already present in the repo — are discovered as "Project Workflows"). No fixture data needs to be created; the checked-in workflow files are sufficient, and none of them need a non-empty `goal` field for the bug to manifest (see step 3).
+- No running Fabro server, no `settings.toml`, no account/credentials required — `fabro workflow list` never contacts a server.
+- Environment variables `TERM=xterm-256color` and `CLICOLOR_FORCE=1` must be set on the command in step 2. Reason: this sandbox has no real tty, so two independent color-enable gates must be forced: `console::colors_enabled_stderr()` (gates the pre-styled title text, checks `CLICOLOR_FORCE` or a real tty) and `cli_table`'s `ColorChoice::Auto` (gates the table body, checks `termcolor::env_allows_color()` — requires `TERM` to be set and not `"dumb"`, and `NO_COLOR` unset). On a real terminal with a genuine dark-background tty, plain `fabro workflow list` reproduces without any env vars — the env vars are a sandbox-only substitute for "has a tty with color support," not part of the bug's trigger condition itself.
+
+**ORDERED ACTIONS**
+1. `cargo build -p fabro-cli` — produces `target/debug/fabro`. (One-time; not required on subsequent runs once the binary exists.)
+2. `TERM=xterm-256color CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 ./target/debug/fabro workflow list 2>&1 | cat -v`
+
+That is the complete minimal sequence — a single command after the build. No further input, flags, or interaction is needed.
+
+**OBSERVED (WRONG) RESULT**
+Every row under "Project Workflows" emits, for the DESCRIPTION cell:
+```
+^[[0m^[[0m ^[[0m^[[0m^[[0m^[[38;5;8m           ^[[0m ^[[0m
+```
+i.e. literal escape `\x1b[38;5;8m` — SGR "set foreground to 256-color palette index 8," an absolute dark-grey palette color, exactly `Color::Ansi256(8)` as reported. This color does not adapt to the terminal's actual background; on a dark-themed terminal it renders text that is nearly the same color as the background (per reporter) and is effectively unreadable.
+
+Contrast check confirms this isn't a global color-suppression artifact: the adjacent NAME cell in the identical row renders `^[[36m` (SGR 36, plain ANSI cyan) — a normal, terminal-relative color — proving color reaches the output stream correctly and the DESCRIPTION column's `38;5;8` is the specific defect, not an environment fluke.
+
+**EXPECTED RESULT**
+The DESCRIPTION cell (and the other nine confirmed call sites — see Code locations) should use a terminal-relative "dim/faint" attribute (SGR 2, `\x1b[2m`) instead of an absolute palette color, so it renders as a dimmed variant of whatever foreground the user's terminal theme actually uses — legible on both light and dark backgrounds. The repo already has this primitive in scope (`fabro_util::terminal::Styles::dim`, and `cli_table::CellStruct::dimmed(bool)` — see Evidence), it's just not applied at these ten sites.
+
+**RELIABILITY**

+# Reproduction report
+
+## Bug
+Secondary/dim text in `fabro` CLI tables (`fabro workflow list`, `fabro ps`, `fabro model list`, `fabro run checkpoints`) is styled with a hardcoded absolute palette color, `Color::Ansi256(8)` ("bright black"), instead of a terminal-relative dim/faint attribute. On a terminal with a dark background this renders the text nearly invisible against the background. In `runs/list.rs`, the same hardcoded color is also used as the STATUS color for `Submitted`/`Pending`/`Dead` runs, and bold is explicitly suppressed for that color — so for those statuses, run state is conveyed only through a color that can be unreadable.
+
+Ten confirmed call sites, all using `.foreground_color(color_if(use_color, Color::Ansi256(8)))` (or, in two `runs/list.rs` cases, the equivalent status-color match):
+- `lib/apps/fabro-cli/src/commands/runs/list.rs:128,138,148,178,184,185`
+- `lib/apps/fabro-cli/src/commands/model.rs:135,138`
+- `lib/apps/fabro-cli/src/commands/workflow/list.rs:113`
+- `lib/apps/fabro-cli/src/commands/run/checkpoints.rs:93`
+
+## Environment / preconditions
+- Repo checked out at current branch tip, working tree clean, cwd = repo root.
+- No running Fabro server, no `settings.toml`, no credentials required — `fabro workflow list` does not contact a server.
+- `.fabro/workflows/*/workflow.toml` (17 project workflow definitions) already present in the repo; none needed modification to trigger the bug.
+- Color output must be enabled through two independent, non-tty gates that both had to be forced in this sandboxed (no real tty) environment:
+  - `CLICOLOR_FORCE=1` — forces `console::colors_enabled_stderr()` (gates the pre-styled title text).
+  - `TERM=xterm-256color` — required so `termcolor::env_allows_color()` (which `cli_table`'s `ColorChoice::Auto` uses) doesn't treat the terminal as unsupported/`"dumb"`.
+  - On a real terminal with a genuine dark-background tty, plain `fabro workflow list` reproduces with no env vars needed — the vars above are a sandbox-only substitute for "has a color-capable tty," not part of the bug's actual trigger condition.
+
+## Reproduction steps
+1. From the repo root, build the CLI: `cargo build -p fabro-cli` (produces `target/debug/fabro`; one-time, not needed on subsequent runs).
+2. Run: `TERM=xterm-256color CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 ./target/debug/fabro workflow list 2>&1 | cat -v`
+
+No other input, flags, fixture data, or interaction is required.
+
+## Observed result
+Every row under "Project Workflows" emits, for the DESCRIPTION cell, the literal escape sequence `\x1b[38;5;8m` — SGR "set foreground to 256-color palette index 8," i.e. exactly `Color::Ansi256(8)` as reported:
+```
+^[[0m^[[0m ^[[0m^[[0m^[[0m^[[38;5;8m           ^[[0m ^[[0m
+```
+This is an absolute dark-grey palette color that does not adapt to the terminal's background theme; on a dark background it renders as effectively unreadable, per the report.
+
+Contrast check confirms this is not a global color-suppression artifact: the adjacent NAME cell in the same row renders `^[[36m` (plain ANSI cyan, terminal-relative) — proving color reaches the output stream correctly and that the DESCRIPTION column's `38;5;8` is the specific defect.
+
+## Expected result
+The DESCRIPTION cell (and the other nine confirmed call sites) should use a terminal-relative dim/faint attribute (SGR 2, `\x1b[2m`) instead of an absolute palette color, so secondary text renders as a dimmed variant of whatever foreground the user's terminal theme actually uses — legible on both light and dark backgrounds.
+
+Resolved the reporter's open technical question by reading crate source: `cli_table::CellStruct` (via the already-imported `Style` trait) exposes `fn dimmed(self, bool) -> Self`, which sets `termcolor::ColorSpec.dimmed` and emits literal `\x1B[2m` — confirmed in `termcolor` 1.4.1 source. This is a terminal-relative attribute, set through the structured `ColorSpec` API rather than by pre-styling the string before `.cell()`, so there is no ANSI-in-column-width measurement concern. `cli-table` 0.5 does support the needed attribute directly.
+

+- `/tmp/wf_list_raw.txt` — initial pty capture of `fabro workflow list` showing the raw escape sequences.
+- `/tmp/repro_confirm.txt` — final confirmation run (2 lines: DESCRIPTION header row and the `card-game` row) showing `\x1b[38;5;8m` around the DESCRIPTION cell, contrasted with `\x1b[36m` on the adjacent NAME cell. Exit code `0` (rendering defect, not a crash).
+- `cli-table` 0.5.0 source (`cell.rs`, `style.rs`) and `termcolor` 1.4.1 source (`src/lib.rs` ~line 1525, `Ansi::set_color`) read directly from the local cargo registry cache, confirming `CellStruct::dimmed(bool)` emits SGR 2.
+- Static verification (not run live — requires a Fabro server not available in this environment) that `runs/list.rs`'s `fn status_cell` (the most severe case: STATUS conveyed only by `Ansi256(8)` for `Submitted`/`Pending`/`Dead`) uses the identical hardcoded-color pattern; code read and confirmed at lines 178, 184, 185.
+
+## Reproduced?
+**Yes.** Reproduces deterministically, 3/3 consecutive runs, byte-identical DESCRIPTION-cell escape sequence each time — not intermittent.
+
+Note: local project workflow files all have empty `goal` fields, so the DESCRIPTION cell text itself is blank in this repro; the hardcoded-color escape sequence still wraps the (empty) cell content identically each run, which is sufficient to confirm the defective call site fires. `fabro ps` (`runs/list.rs`, the most severe STATUS-color case) could not be driven live in this environment (no running Fabro server available) and was verified statically by reading the code instead — its code path (`color_if(use_color, Color::Ansi256(8))` / identical status-color match) is the same mechanism confirmed live in `workflow/list.rs`.
